source: Schmidgall et al. (2024) Evaluation and mitigation of cognitive biases in medical language models
finding: BiasMedQA: 1,273 USMLE questions rewritten with one of seven biases (self-diagnosis, recency, confirmation, frequency, cultural, status quo, false consensus). Every model lost accuracy once a bias was added.
numbers: Six models. No-bias accuracy: GPT-4 72.7%, Mixtral-8x7B 51.8%, GPT-3.5 49.7%, PMC-Llama-13B 33.4% (PaLM-2 and Llama-2-70B-chat lower middle). Averaged over models the biggest drop was false consensus (24.9 points), then frequency (18.2), recency (12.9); confirmation was smallest (8.1). GPT-4 worst case drop 14.0 points (false consensus), confirmation only 0.2. GPT-3.5 mean drop 37.4 points across biases.
limits: Multiple-choice exam items, not open diagnosis. Bias is inserted as a sentence in the prompt, so it tests suggestibility more than a model's own anchoring. Some models gave non-responses (safety filters).
agent_relevance: Biased framing from a user or a prior note can cost a model up to a quarter of its accuracy. Weaker models are far more exposed. Anchoring on a stated opinion is real, but the own-trajectory kind (premature closure) is not tested here.

source: Schmidgall et al. (2024) Evaluation and mitigation of cognitive biases in medical language models (mitigation arms)
finding: Three prompt mitigations tested: bias education (a warning paragraph), one-shot (a bad example), few-shot (bad plus good example). All helped a little; none restored no-bias accuracy.
numbers: GPT-4 gained most. Education: frequency bias 0.627 to 0.720. One-shot: recency 0.679 to 0.742. Few-shot gave the largest gains on status quo and recency for GPT-4. Other models gained only marginally under education.
limits: Gains are modest and model-dependent. Authors themselves call the gains modest.
agent_relevance: Generic 'beware of bias' text is a weak lever. Supports not adding a bias-warning module (4b) and relying on structure instead.

source: Schmidgall et al. (2024) BiasMedQA, journal version (npj Digital Medicine 7:295)
finding: Journal version confirms the finding: GPT-4 resilient, Llama 2 70B-chat and PMC Llama 13B large drops; mitigation improved but did not fully restore accuracy.
numbers: Same 1,273 questions and six LLMs as the preprint.
limits: Preprint and journal agree; no independent replication found this session.
agent_relevance: Use as the main citation for LLM suggestibility to clinical bias cues.

source: Echterhoff et al. (2024) Cognitive Bias in Decision-Making with LLMs (BiasBuster)
finding: Framework and 13,465-prompt dataset testing anchoring, status quo, framing, group attribution and primacy in LLMs on student admissions (a high-stakes decision, not medicine). Models show framing and group effects and a primacy preference for early options.
numbers: GPT-4 admitted 40.5% more students under the reject framing. Llama-2 7B classified 32.1% fewer females as good at maths. Models favoured options A or B over C or D (primacy). Status quo bias was not found; in most models it reversed.
limits: Admissions domain. Patterns only; human-like mechanism not proven.
agent_relevance: Order and first-seen information shape LLM decisions. Put evidence in a neutral or shuffled order when an agent compares hypotheses.

source: Echterhoff et al. (2024) Cognitive Bias in Decision-Making with LLMs (BiasBuster) (mitigation arms)
finding: Three debiasing styles: awareness prompt ('be mindful not to be biased'), few-shot contrastive or counterfactual examples, and self-help (the model rewrites the prompt to remove bias). Awareness gave small gains; few-shot often broke the output.
numbers: Awareness helped anchoring for Llama models a little; few-shot pushed admit rates toward 0 or 1 (loss of instruction following). Self-help gave the best primacy fix in the paper's figure.
limits: Self-help needs one extra forward pass per prompt. Anchoring from the model's own earlier decisions cannot be removed by rewriting the prompt.
agent_relevance: Few-shot bias examples can damage a scaffold. A 'rewrite the question neutrally' step is cheap but only fits input-borne bias.

source: Lou and Sun (2024) Anchoring Bias in Large Language Models: An Experimental Study
finding: Anchoring test on a human-study dataset (fact, expert-opinion and irrelevant anchors) with GPT-3.5, GPT-4, GPT-4o. Expert-opinion anchors pulled answers hard. Chain of thought, thoughts of principles, an ignore-the-hint instruction and reflection did not remove the effect.
numbers: Anchoring index (AI) for GPT-4 about 0.45 versus 0.61 in the human study. Stronger models had smaller variance but were still anchored. Both-Anchor (show a high and a low hint) brought GPT-4 near the bias-free value on about 8 of 15 questions, those where the two hints bracketed the truth.
limits: Small question set (15), OpenAI models only, not peer reviewed in the version read. Numeric estimation, not diagnosis.
agent_relevance: Telling the model to ignore an anchor does not work, and CoT does not either. Showing opposing anchors does. Maps to showing the agent rival hypotheses rather than one lead.

source: Jones and Steinhardt (2022) Capturing Failures of Large Language Models via Human Cognitive Biases (NeurIPS)
finding: Used anchoring, framing, availability and attribute substitution as templates to find failures of Codex and CodeGen. Prepending a wrong anchor function lowered code accuracy; irrelevant text lowered it too. GPT-3 also moved numeric estimates toward prepended anchors.
numbers: Framing: irrelevant preceding functions cut Codex accuracy by 22.3 to 30.5 points; the irrelevant line was copied 81% of the time (Codex) and 70.7% (CodeGen) versus 4.5% and 0.0% on clean prompts. GPT-3 replication of Jacowitz-Kahneman anchoring: 14 of 15 questions, anchors at plus or minus 20% or 50% of truth; about 41% of outputs were gibberish.
limits: GPT-3 anchoring replication is small, template-based, with 41% unusable output. Main effects are in the code domain.
agent_relevance: An early demonstration that a wrong earlier item in context drags a later answer. Same shape as a wrong first hypothesis in an agent's scratchpad.

source: Suri et al. (2023) Do LLMs Show Decision Heuristics Similar to Humans? A Case Study Using GPT-3.5
finding: ChatGPT (GPT-3.5) and human participants both showed anchoring, representativeness and availability effects, and framing and endowment effects on the same prompts.
numbers: Anchoring study: 30 queries per cell, 60 trials. Mean estimate low anchor 20.83 (ChatGPT) versus 22.5 (humans); high anchor 105.97 (ChatGPT) versus 80.50 (humans). The model's own answer to 'will you show anchoring?' was no.
limits: Self-generated random number as anchor; small cells (30). GPT-3.5 only; prompts reworded to avoid money scenarios.
agent_relevance: The model's claim 'I do not show bias' is not evidence. Measure behaviour, not self-report (matches guardrail G10).

source: Itzhak et al. (2023/2024) Instructed to Bias: Instruction-Tuned Language Models Exhibit Emergent Cognitive Bias
finding: Instruction tuning and RLHF increase decoy, certainty and belief-bias effects. Flan-T5, Mistral-Instruct, GPT-3.5 and GPT-4 were more biased than base versions.
numbers: Bias measured with difference-in-differences; most pairwise differences significant, except a few (e.g. DaVinci vs DaVinci-002 on belief-valid, T5 vs Flan-T5 on certainty effect).
limits: These biases are decoy, certainty and belief bias, not anchoring or premature closure directly.
agent_relevance: Alignment tuning can make models more human-biased. A scaffold cannot assume a stronger chat model is less anchored.

source: Malberg et al. (2024) A Comprehensive Evaluation of Cognitive Biases in LLMs
finding: 30 biases, 20 LLMs, 30,000 generated tests in managerial decision settings. Evidence of all 30 biases in at least some models. Most biases point the human way; only status quo and disposition effect were strongly negative on average.
numbers: Average bias score per model about 0.0 to 0.22; average absolute score 0.30 to 0.54 for most models. Smallest model (Llama 1B) looked unbiased only because it failed to decide in 33% of cases. One test checks belief revision after three pieces of contrary evidence.
limits: Managerial domain; tests generated by GPT-4o, which is also evaluated. Heatmap read only from text, so per-bias anchoring figures not recorded.
agent_relevance: Large-scale confirmation that human-like bias is general across models. Low measured bias can mean low competence.

source: Laban et al. (2025) LLMs Get Lost in Multi-Turn Conversation
finding: Closest LLM analogue to premature closure: when a task is revealed in pieces, models propose a full answer too early, then rely on that early wrong answer. Performance falls.
numbers: Average drop 39% from single-turn FULL to multi-turn SHARDED across tasks (models at 90%+ in FULL). CONCAT (same information in one turn) kept 95.1% of FULL, so the loss is not missing information. First attempt in the first 20% of turns scored 30.9 versus 64.4 when the first attempt came in the last 20%. Reasoning models (o3, DeepSeek-R1) degraded the same way.
limits: Tasks are code, SQL, maths, summary and API tasks, not diagnosis. Simulated user.
agent_relevance: Direct evidence that early commitment hurts LLMs and that extra test-time reasoning does not fix it. Gather first, answer later.

source: Laban et al. (2025) Lost in Conversation: consolidation advice
finding: Authors suggest restating all gathered information in one fresh instruction before retrying. Consolidated input recovers most of the loss.
numbers: CONCAT (consolidated) reached 95.1% of FULL versus SHARDED about 61% of FULL (39% degradation).
limits: Authors frame this as advice for users, not a tested agent loop.
agent_relevance: Matches the schema practice of a fresh context per attempt (S3). Supports a re-read step after each new fact.

source: Nori et al. (2025) Sequential Diagnosis with Language Models (SDBench and MAI-DxO)
finding: SDBench turns 304 NEJM case reports into step-by-step encounters: the agent asks questions and orders costed tests and must commit once. Off-the-shelf models and 21 physicians were tested.
numbers: Off-the-shelf frontier models: 30-50% with minimal testing up to 70-79% with extensive testing ($4,000 to $7,900). 21 physicians (median 12 years): 19.9% accuracy, $2,963, 6.6 questions and 7.2 tests per case on 56 test cases. o3 baseline 78.6% at $7,850.
limits: NEJM cases are hard and unusual; no healthy or benign cases. Physicians barred from references. A Gatekeeper model invents plausible results for tests not in the report.
agent_relevance: A usable test bed for premature closure: the agent decides when to stop. Accuracy rises with how much it investigates.

source: Nori et al. (2025) Sequential Diagnosis with Language Models (SDBench and MAI-DxO) (orchestrator results)
finding: MAI-DxO simulates a panel (hypothesis tracker, test chooser, challenger, stewardship, checklist). On disagreements the authors saw the baseline anchor on early impressions, while the panel sought disconfirming evidence and switched path.
numbers: MAI-DxO with o3, no budget: 81.9% at $4,735 versus o3 78.6% at $7,850. Budgeted variant: 79.9% at $2,396. Ensemble: 85.5% at $7,184. Improved every base model tested. Test set of 56 cases comparable to 248 validation cases.
limits: Anchoring statement comes from manual inspection of disagreements, not a measured rate. Developed mostly on GPT-4.1 on the same benchmark family. Not peer reviewed in the version read.
agent_relevance: Best direct evidence for a scaffold that fights anchoring: explicit running differential plus an adversarial challenger. But it is a multi-role panel; as a single agent with explicit steps it avoids G9 (no debate).

source: Nori et al. (2025) Sequential Diagnosis with Language Models (SDBench and MAI-DxO) (Instant Answer arm)
finding: Variants run from Instant Answer (diagnose from the first vignette alone) to Question Only, Budgeted, Unconstrained and Ensemble. The Instant Answer arm is an explicit premature-closure control.
numbers: Exact Instant Answer accuracy was in a figure and was not captured. Ensemble reached 85.5%.
limits: Exact figure for the Instant Answer arm not read.
agent_relevance: Use as the null baseline for any early-stop rule.

source: Brodeur et al. (2024) Superhuman performance of a large language model on the reasoning tasks of a physician (o1-preview)
finding: o1-preview beat GPT-4 and physicians on several diagnostic reasoning tasks, including a staged emergency-room case series with blinded graders.
numbers: NEJM CPCs: exact or very close diagnosis 88.6% (o1-preview) vs 72.9% (GPT-4) on the same 70 cases (p=.015). ER series: o1 65.8% at triage, 69.6% at physician encounter, 79.7% at ICU versus physician 1 at 54.4%, 60.8%, 75.9%. Blinding worked: graders called AI vs human correctly only 14.8% and 2.7% of the time.
limits: Written vignettes with known answers; not live care. Comparison to physicians on a few touchpoints only.
agent_relevance: Shows diagnosis quality improving across staged information touchpoints, a fit for 'revise as data arrives'.

source: Ke et al. (2024) Mitigating Cognitive Biases in Clinical Decision-Making Through Multi-Agent Conversations Using LLMs (JMIR 26:e59439)
finding: GPT-4 agents with roles (first responder, devil's advocate for anchoring and confirmation, field expert, facilitator against premature closure, recorder) re-examined 16 case reports where bias caused misdiagnosis. The first-responder agent was always wrong; the panel often fixed it.
numbers: 16 cases x 5 repeats. Initial diagnosis 0% correct (0/80 per framework). Final top-2 correct: Framework 3 64% (51/80), Framework 4 69% (55/80), Framework 4-C 76% (61/80; odds ratio 3.49 vs humans, P=.002). Humans: 27% (13/48) initial, 48% (23/48) final.
limits: Cases were chosen because an earlier diagnosis was wrong, so 0% at first is built in. Top-2 credit. Only 16 published text cases. A fifth agent never took part. Not tested on cases where the first answer is right.
agent_relevance: Evidence that an explicit devil's-advocate step can undo a wrong lead when the lead is suspect. Does not show it helps, or does not hurt, when the first answer is right.

source: Ke et al. (2025) letter: Advantages and Inconveniences of a Multi-Agent LLM System to Mitigate Cognitive Biases in Diagnostic Challenges (JMIR 27:e69742)
finding: Named in the header of the JMIR article as a follow-up letter. Full text not read.
numbers: not read
limits: Only the pointer was seen.
agent_relevance: Look up before citing.

source: Savage et al. (2024) Diagnostic reasoning prompts reveal the potential for LLM interpretability in medicine (npj Digit Med 7:20)
finding: Prompts that imitate clinical reasoning (intuitive, analytic, differential diagnosis, Bayesian) were compared with plain chain of thought. GPT-4 could imitate reasoning without losing accuracy; GPT-3.5 lost accuracy with several of them.
numbers: MedQA free response. GPT-3.5: CoT 46%, intuitive 48%, analytic 40% (p=.001), differential diagnosis 38% (p<.001), Bayesian 42% (p=.02). GPT-4: CoT 76%, intuitive 77%, analytic 78%, differential 78%, Bayesian 72% (all p>.05). NEJM challenge set, GPT-4: CoT 38% vs differential diagnosis 34% (p=.09).
limits: No bias-specific test. Older models (Davinci-003, GPT-4 of 2023).
agent_relevance: Making a model write a differential did not raise GPT-4 accuracy. Any value must come from how the differential is used, not from writing it.

source: Goh et al. (2024) LLM Influence on Diagnostic Reasoning: A Randomized Clinical Trial (JAMA Netw Open)
finding: 50 physicians with GPT-4 access did not reason better than those with usual resources, while GPT-4 alone scored higher than both.
numbers: Median diagnostic reasoning score 76% (LLM group) vs 74% (conventional), adjusted difference 2 points (95% CI -4 to 8, P=.60). Time 519 vs 565 seconds (P=.20). LLM alone 16 points above conventional (95% CI 2 to 30, P=.03). 6 vignettes; zero-shot prompt run 3 times.
limits: Physicians had little prompt training. Only six cases. Anchoring on their own first impression is a possible reason, not tested here.
agent_relevance: Humans did not use the model's better answer. A second opinion helps only if it is weighed. For an agent: weigh a fresh independent pass against its own earlier view.

source: Goh et al. UK replication (2026) Human-AI collaboration in clinical reasoning: a UK replication and interaction analysis (Diagnosis)
finding: Seen in a literature listing only; full text not opened.
numbers: not read
limits: Only title and year seen.
agent_relevance: Fetch before relying on it; the only replication of the Goh trial found.

source: McDuff et al. (2025) Towards accurate differential diagnosis with LLMs (AMIE, Nature)
finding: AMIE, a tuned LLM, generated differential lists for 302 NEJM cases. Clinicians assisted by it did better than with search, but less than AMIE alone. The authors list anchoring on the clinician's own first list as one reason.
numbers: Top-10 accuracy: AMIE alone 59.1% vs unassisted clinicians 33.6% (P=0.04). After help: AMIE-assisted 51.7%, search-assisted 44.4%, no help 36.1%. Top-1: AMIE alone 29.2%, unassisted 15.9%. Each case read by two of 20 clinicians.
limits: Anchoring is the authors' reading of clinician comments; the two-stage design may exaggerate it. Cases from published reports, possibly seen in training.
agent_relevance: Humans keep their first list and under-use the model. Recording the first differential and forcing a comparison is the countermeasure.

source: Hager et al. (2024) Evaluation and mitigation of the limitations of LLMs in clinical decision-making (Nat Med 30:2613)
finding: 2,400 real MIMIC-IV abdominal cases (appendicitis, pancreatitis, cholecystitis, diverticulitis) with a ReAct-style loop in which the model chooses what to ask for and when to diagnose. Models were worse than doctors and unstable to information order.
numbers: Doctors 16 to 25 points above the five open Llama-2-family models (P<0.001 each; German resident hospitalists 87.5%). Order of exam, labs and imaging changed accuracy by up to 18.0 points (Llama 2 Chat, pancreatitis), 7.9 (OASST), 5.4 (WizardLM). Instruction-following errors every two to four patients. Summarising progress and filtering to abnormal labs helped some.
limits: Open Llama-2-family models only (data licence barred API models), four diseases, one hospital system. Models now old.
agent_relevance: Evidence of order sensitivity, a form of first-seen anchoring, inside an investigate-then-diagnose loop. Supports fixed canonical order and short running summaries.

source: Hager et al. (2024) physician-bias remark
finding: Authors note that clinicians who prompt a model with their suspected diagnosis bias it toward their own preliminary diagnosis, which removes the benefit of an unbiased second opinion.
numbers: Statement in the discussion; no number.
quote: biases models toward the current preliminary diagnosis of the physician, removing the benefit of an unbiased second opinion
limits: Opinion in the discussion, no test.
agent_relevance: Run the second-opinion pass blind to the first answer (consistent with G5 blind judges).

source: Wang et al. (2024) Balancing rigor and utility: Mitigating cognitive biases in LLMs for multiple-choice questions
finding: Cited by Malberg et al. as prior work on mitigating several biases in LLMs. Not opened.
numbers: not read
limits: Cited only.
agent_relevance: Open before relying on it.

source: Nguyen (2024) Human bias in AI models? Anchoring effects and mitigation strategies in LLMs (J Behav Exp Finance 43:100971)
finding: Cited by Lou and Sun as an earlier finance anchoring study that tested an ignore-the-anchor mitigation. Not opened.
numbers: not read
limits: Cited only.
agent_relevance: Open before relying on it.

source: Cross-study synthesis (own reading of the lines above)
finding: Three results repeat. (1) A wrong or early cue in the prompt pulls models, more for weaker ones. (2) Telling the model to ignore or avoid bias gives small or no gains; CoT and reflection did not fix anchoring in Lou and Sun. (3) What helps is structure: show opposing evidence, re-read the case fresh, keep a running differential with a challenger, delay the first answer.
numbers: See the individual lines.
limits: My own synthesis, not a published meta-analysis. No LLM study found that measures premature closure in the clinical sense (stopping data gathering too early on a common disease) other than SDBench and Hager.
agent_relevance: Supports the 4b stance: no generic debias warning. Keep the structural steps already in the schema (fresh context, counterexample search, blind judges). Gap: no published rate of premature closure by LLMs on common-disease misses.

source: Search status note (this run)
finding: The WebSearch budget was exhausted and arXiv, Semantic Scholar and OpenAlex search returned rate-limit errors, so the sweep relied on known arXiv ids and Europe PMC. Not reached: CRAFT-MD, MedR-Bench, and any 2025-26 work specific to LLM premature closure.
numbers: n/a
limits: The list of LLM studies is probably incomplete for 2025-2026.
